'''''Lagerstroemia indica''''', known as the '''[[crape myrtle]]''' (also '''crepe myrtle''', '''crêpe myrtle''', or '''crepeflower'''<ref>{{cite web |url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?id=21393 |title=USDA GRIN Taxonomy |website=Npgsweb.ars-grin.gov |access-date=8 June 2016 }}</ref>), is a species of flowering plant in the genus ''[[Lagerstroemia]]'' of the family [[Lythraceae]]. It is native to East Asia, South Asia and Southeast Asia.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Lagerstroemia indica'' |url=https://www.nparks.gov.sg/florafaunaweb/flora/2/1/2173 |website=www.nparks.gov.sg }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Macquarie University |first1=Sydney |title=Crepe Myrtle ''Lagerstroemia indica'' |url=https://www.mq.edu.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0003/1335252/Lagerstroemia-indica-2025.pdf |website=mq.edu.au |publisher=Macquarie University |access-date=15 October 2023 }}</ref><ref name="553576-1" >{{cite POWO |id=553576-1 |title=''Lagerstroemia indica'' L. |access-date=9 April 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=张 |first=启翔 |date=1991 |title=紫薇品种分类及其在园林中的应用(英文) |url=http://kns.cnki.net/KCMS/detail/detail.aspx?dbcode=CJFD&filename=BJLY199104008 |journal=北京林业大学学报 |issue=4 |pages=57–66 |issn=1000-1522 }}</ref> It is an often multi-stemmed, [[deciduous]] tree with a wide spreading, flat topped, rounded, or even spike shaped open habit. The tree is a popular nesting shrub for songbirds and wrens.

==Description==
[[File:US Capitol with flowers 2016.jpg|thumb|Crape myrtle blooming near the [[United States Capitol]]]]
[[File:Lagerstroemia indica 4.jpg|thumb|Inflorescence]]
[[File:Lagerstroemia indica MHNT.BOT.2025.29.3.jpg|thumb|''Lagerstroemia indica'' ([[MHNT]])]]
[[File:Extremosa com flores brancas - 55007156862.jpg|thumb|Crape myrtle with white flowers in Brazil]]

The bark is thin and about {{cvt|2|mm|frac=16}} thick, smooth, pinkish-gray and mottled, shedding each year. Leaves also shed each winter, after spectacular color display, and bare branches re-leaf early in the spring; leaves are small, smooth-edged, circular or oval-shaped, and dark green changing to yellow and orange and red in autumn.

Flowers, on different trees, are white, pink, mauve, purple or carmine with crimped petals, in [[panicles]] up to {{cvt|9|cm|in|frac=2}}. Flowers give way to 6-capsuled, brown dehiscent fruits.<ref>{{Cite web |title=''Lagerstroemia indica'' (Crapemyrtle, Crape Myrtle, Crepe Myrtle) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/lagerstroemia-indica/ |access-date=9 March 2021 |website=Plants.ces.ncsu.edu }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Lagerstroemia indica'' is native to the [[subtropical]] regions of Asia; the [[Himalayan subtropical broadleaf forests]] in Nepal, India, Bhutan, Bangladesh, southern China, [[mainland Southeast Asia]], Taiwan, the Philippines, and Japan.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="553576-1" />

''Lagerstroemia'' is a common planting in [[South Atlantic States]] and is becoming an increasingly common shrub in [[Mid-Atlantic states|Mid-Atlantic]] states all the way up through the coastal areas of Massachusetts.<ref>{{cite news |author=Hilary Newell |date=13 September 2012 |title=Crape Myrtle - A Great Late Season Shrub |newspaper=Nantucket Chronicle |url=https://www.nantucketchronicle.com/gardening-landscaping/2012/crape-myrtle-a-great-late-season-shrub |access-date=11 December 2017 |archive-date=2 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200802231143/https://www.nantucketchronicle.com/gardening-landscaping/2012/crape-myrtle-a-great-late-season-shrub |url-status=dead }}</ref> ''Lagerstroemia indica'' is listed as invasive in certain natural areas.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Reichard, Sarah. 1994. Assessing the potential of invasiveness in woody plants introduced in North America. University of Washington Ph.D. dissertation.: Invasive Plant Atlas of the United States |url=https://www.invasiveplantatlas.org/list.html?id=131 |access-date=8 April 2026 |website=www.invasiveplantatlas.org }}</ref>

==Cultivation==
In the United States, ''Lagerstroemia indica'' is a very popular flowering shrub/small tree in mild-winter states ([[Hardiness zone|USDA Zones]] 6–10).<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=''Lagerstroemia indica'' - Plant Finder |url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=282496&isprofile=1&basic=lagerstroemia%20indica |access-date=9 March 2021 |website=Missouribotanicalgarden.org }}</ref> Low maintenance needs make it a common municipal planting in parks, along sidewalks, highway medians and in parking lots. Like the [[southern magnolia]], the crape myrtle has come to symbolize the [[Southern United States|American South]] because of its extensive planting and ability to thrive in hot, humid summer climates with regular precipitation.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.southernliving.com/home-garden/gardens/southern-gardening-crepe-myrtle-history |title=History of Crape Myrtles in the South |author=Steve Bender |publisher=Southern Living |access-date=31 May 2017 }}</ref> It is one of only a few trees/shrubs to offer brilliant color in late summer through autumn, at a time when many flowering plants have exhausted their blooms. In arid climates, it requires supplemental watering and some shade in the very hottest areas. The plant must have hot summers in order to flower successfully, otherwise it will show weak bloom and is more vulnerable to fungal diseases.<ref name = "Brenzel" >{{cite book |title=Sunset Western Garden Book |editor=Kathleen Norris Brenzel |year=2007 |page=430 }}</ref>

Frequently ''L. indica'' is root hardy to Zone 5 ({{cvt|-10|F|order=flip|disp=or}}), meaning it will be killed back during harsh winters but regrow from the roots and flower in summer. As such Northern gardeners treat it more like a perennial than a tree or shrub. Too much watering and over-fertilizing can decrease the cold hardiness because it stimulates new growth late in the season that does not have time to harden off.<ref name = "Brenzel" />

''Lagerstroemia indica'' is frost tolerant, prefers full sun and will grow to {{cvt|20|feet|m|0|order=flip}} with a spread of {{cvt|20|feet|m|0|order=flip}}. The plant is not picky about soil type but does require good drainage to thrive. Once established it is also quite drought hardy, though it benefits from the occasional deep watering during the summer months.<ref name = "Brenzel" />

15 [[hybrid (biology)#In plants|hybrid]] [[cultivars]] have been developed between ''L. indica'' and ''L. fauriei'' by the [[US National Arboretum]] for increased cold-hardiness and resistance to disease, all given the names of Native American tribes.<ref name = "Brenzel" /> There are also dwarf cultivars of ''indica'' × ''fauriei'' cross-breeds and regular ''L. indica'' species, which grow {{cvt|2-5|ft|m|1|order=flip}}.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/home/choosing-the-right-crape-myrtle/2015/03/17/cf406e8a-c758-11e4-a199-6cb5e63819d2_story.html |title=How to choose the right crape myrtle |author=Adrian Higgins |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=18 March 2015 |access-date=1 June 2017 }}</ref>

=== Pests and diseases ===
In the Southern U.S. mildew and fungal diseases have traditionally posed problems for ''L.{{nbs}}indica''. This was a major motivation for developing the ''[[Lagerstroemia indica × L. fauriei]]'' hybrids, which show increased resistance to [[powdery mildew]] and fungus. The fungal pathogen ''[[Cercospora lythracearum]]'' can infest the plant in summer during hot, rainy weather and cause premature leaf drop. Gardeners plant resistant hybrid varieties or use fungicide sprays to help control this.<ref name="usna.usda.gov">{{cite news |url=http://www.usna.usda.gov/Gardens/faqs/crapemyrtlefaq2.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020904214008/http://www.usna.usda.gov/Gardens/faqs/crapemyrtlefaq2.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=4 September 2002 |title=Crape Myrtle Questions & Answers - US National Arboretum - USDA |website=Usna.usda.gov |date=14 October 2004 |access-date=31 May 2017 }}</ref>

Insect problems with ''Lagestroemia indica'' include the crape myrtle aphid, ''[[Tinocallis kahawaluokalani]]'', which can cause yellow spots and black mold, [[Japanese beetles]], and the [[flea beetle]]. None of these insects are fatal to the plant and other predator insects are usually enough to resolve infestations; however applications of [[insecticidal soap]] can also be helpful.<ref name="usna.usda.gov"/>

=== Crape myrtle topping ===
During the winter, gardeners will often lop off the branches of large specimens, to manage size and encourage more profuse summer bloom. This is colloquially known as "crape murder" because of the drastic pruning involved, leaving a bare trunk during the winter and early spring.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/home/dont-commit-a-crape-murder/2015/03/17/269d2508-c446-11e4-9ec2-b418f57a4a99_story.html |title=How to avoid hacking at your crape myrtle this spring |author=Adrian Higgins |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=8 March 2015 |access-date=31 May 2017 }}</ref> [[Tree topping]] of crape myrtles is a common occurrence, but is not recommended nor endorsed by many professional standards or arboricultural organizations.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.saiglobal.com/PDFTemp/Previews/OSH/AS/AS4000/4300/4373-2007.pdf |title=Australian Standard : Pruning of amenity trees |website=Saiglobal.com |access-date=22 March 2022 }}</ref>

==Culture==
In 1983, [[Hinako Sugiura]] started a manga series titled ''[[Sarusuberi]]'', after the Japanese name of the plant.
Sugiura compared the flowering season of ''L. indica'', that keeps blooming and dropping flowers at the same time, with the vigor of [[ukiyo-e]] art, the setting of the manga.<ref name="Yumemakura">[[Hinako Sugiura]] in the first volume of the 1985 [[Jitsugyo no Nihonsha]] edition. Quoted in 1996 by Baku Yumemakura in {{cite book |last1=Sugiura |first1=Hinako |title=Miss Hokusai |date=2018 |publisher=Ponent Mon |isbn=9788492444670 |page=354 |language=es }}</ref> In 2018, the cultivar [[L. indica 'Lingmeng'|''L. indica'' 'Lingmeng']] became widely known in China after people noticed the resemblance of its flowers to a video game character's outfit.<ref name="IGN Japan">{{Cite web |last=Leung |first=Au Yeung Yu |date=30 April 2018 |script-title=ja:「東方Project」の人気キャラが新品種の花の正式名称に!中華娯楽週報 第14回: 全中華の至る所で咲き乱れるACGオタクたち |url=https://jp.ign.com/china-weekly/24375/project-14acg |access-date=21 August 2026|website=IGN Japan |language=ja}}</ref>

The crape myrtle is [[List of Texas state symbols|Texas' official state non-native shrub]].
